title: Radar evidence of an accessible cave conduit on the Moon below the Mare Tranquillitatis pit
authors: L. Carrer, R. Pozzobon, F. Sauro, D. Castelletti, G. Senn, E. Ferro, L. Bruzzone
summary: Analysed radar reflections from the 2010 Mini-RF dataset using complex simulation models of radar interaction with subsurface features. Concludes that an initial conduit segment 30-80 meters long extends from the west floor of the Mare Tranquillitatis Pit (MTP), descending at an angle into a horizontal lava tube.
key_takeaways: First direct observational evidence of an accessible subsurface conduit on the Moon.
The conduit roof thickness is estimated at tens of meters, providing radiation and micrometeorite shielding.
Radar sounders detect lateral cavities when oriented obliquely to the pit entrance.

title: Chandrayaan-2 Dual-frequency Synthetic Aperture Radar (DFSAR): Performance Characterization and Initial Results
authors: S. Bhiravarasu, N. Chakraborty, D. Putrevu, D. K. Pandey, et al.
summary: Describes the performance and operational modes of the DFSAR on ISRO's Chandrayaan-2 orbiter. Operates in L-band (1.25 GHz) and S-band (2.5 GHz) in full and compact polarimetry modes with spatial resolution down to 2 m.
key_takeaways: L-band penetrates deeper into lunar regolith (several meters) than S-band or optical sensors.
Circular Polarization Ratio (CPR) and m-chi polarimetric decomposition distinguish surface blockiness from subsurface scattering.
Caution: Radar backscatter variations alone do not directly confirm underground cavities without multi-angle validation.

title: Automated Lunar Crater Identification with Chandrayaan-2 TMC-2 Images using Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
authors: S. Sinha, S. Paul, S. Ghosh, S. Mohanty
summary: Applies convolutional neural networks and U-Net variants to Chandrayaan-2 Terrain Mapping Camera-2 (TMC-2) imagery and derived DEMs for autonomous crater and depression segmentation across lunar maria and highlands.
key_takeaways: TMC-2 stereo triplets generate 5-meter resolution lunar elevation models.
Combined optical + DEM gradient input achieves higher F1 scores for depression boundaries than optical alone.
Geographic test splits are vital to prevent spatial overfitting to single lighting conditions.

title: The structural stability of lunar lava tubes
authors: D. M. Blair, L. Chappaz, R. Sood, C. Milbury, A. Bobet, H. J. Melosh, B. C. Johnson, P. J. McGovern
summary: Investigated the maximum sustainable dimensions of lunar lava tubes using 2D and 3D finite element models with basalt rock mechanical properties under 1/6th lunar gravity (g = 1.62 m/s²).
key_takeaways: In lunar gravity, uncollapsed lava tubes with spans exceeding 1 km to 5 km can remain stable with roof thicknesses of 30-100 m.
Stability is limited by tensile failure at the center of the roof (crown) and shear failure at the springlines.
Arching action in intact basalt formations redistributes lithostatic stresses around the cavern.

title: Lunar lava tubes: Morphology to structural stability
authors: A. K. Theinat, A. Modiriasari, A. Bobet, H. J. Melosh
summary: Refined lunar lava tube structural modeling by incorporating realistic non-circular cross sections (elliptical, lenticular, semi-circular), variable overburden thickness, and rock mass rating (RMR) discontinuous behavior.
key_takeaways: Arched and semi-circular roofs exhibit significantly higher factors of safety than flat roofs.
Roof tensile stresses scale with (span / thickness)² under self-weight gravity load.
Overhanging edges around skylights (pits) are the most vulnerable zone for secondary collapses.

title: Structural stability of lunar lava tubes with consideration of variable cross-section geometry
authors: M. Chwała, N. Komatsu, J. Haruyama
summary: Evaluates 3D structural stability of basaltic lava conduits under varying wall-thickness, asymmetric cross-sections, and lunar seismic acceleration.
key_takeaways: Irregular and asymmetrical cross-sections induce local stress concentrations at the corners.
Seismic peak ground acceleration (PGA) from moonquakes decreases the factor of safety by 15-25% in thin-roof segments.

title: Lunar pits: Distribution, morphology, and exploration targets
authors: R. V. Wagner, M. S. Robinson
summary: Comprehensive catalog of over 200 lunar pits identified using LROC NAC imagery. Classified into mare pits (suspected collapse into lava tubes), impact melt pits, and highland collapse pits.
key_takeaways: Marius Hills Hole (14.09°N, 303.28°E) and Mare Tranquillitatis Pit (8.33°N, 33.22°E) show sub-surface overhangs extending beyond the illuminated rim.
Pit walls expose stratified basalt flows providing crucial clues about mare volcanism and roof thickness.

title: Evidence of large empty lava tubes on the Moon using GRAIL gravity
authors: L. Chappaz, R. Sood, H. J. Melosh, K. C. Howell, D. M. Blair, C. Milbury, M. T. Zuber
summary: Used high-resolution gravitational gradients from NASA's GRAIL mission to detect mass deficits associated with buried lunar lava tubes in Oceanus Procellarum and Mare Serenitatis.
key_takeaways: Candidate lava tubes detected with widths of 1 km or more based on negative gravity gradient anomalies.
Gravity data provides independent verification that can complement radar and optical imagery.
